analysis.one_liner: Lets insurers sell individual health plans nationwide under one state's rules instead of each state's.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: Senator Heller introduced it with zero cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate health committee, and it never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let a health insurer pick one 'primary' state and sell individual health insurance in every other state under that state's rules, rather than each state's own rules. Insurers would be exempt from other states' laws governing benefits, pricing, and underwriting, though states could still tax them, examine their finances, and police fraud and claim-handling. The bill required a bold-print notice telling buyers the policy may cost less because it is not subject to all of their state's consumer protections or required benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, health insurers would gain the most: they could shop for the state with the loosest rules on mandated benefits, medical underwriting, and rate changes, and sell those leaner policies everywhere. Healthy buyers who want bare-bones, cheaper coverage would have more options. Insurers in permissive states could expand nationwide without meeting 49 other states' licensing and coverage rules.

how_it_helps.text: An insurer could designate one state as its 'primary state' and have that state's laws govern its individual health plans sold in every other state, exempting it from secondary states' laws on rating, underwriting, renewal, and issuance of coverage.

The bill does include some guardrails: insurers cannot raise an individual's premium at renewal based on health status, must meet a risk-based capital floor, must offer independent external appeals for denied claims, and must print a prominent warning that the policy may be cheaper because it skips the selling state's mandated benefits and consumer protections.

Secondary states keep limited powers: they can tax the insurer, require registration, examine its finances if the primary state has not, compel participation in insolvency guaranty funds, and enforce laws against fraud and unfair claims-settlement practices.
Supporters' stated aim was to expand choices and lower prices for people buying their own coverage, by letting them buy plans regulated by less restrictive states.

analysis.who_pays: People buying coverage who need the protections their state now provides — mandated benefits, restrictions on rate changes, and network and quality rules — would lose them when buying an out-of-state plan. People with preexisting conditions could face higher premiums as insurers draw healthy customers into thinly regulated plans and leave costlier patients in state-regulated pools. State insurance regulators would lose authority over policies sold to their own residents, since the primary state would have sole jurisdiction to enforce the governing rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own required disclosure tells buyers a policy 'may be less expensive than others because it is not subject to all of the insurance laws and regulations' of their state, 'including coverage of some services or benefits mandated by the law' of their state, and is 'not subject to all of the consumer protection laws or restrictions on rate changes' of their state — an acknowledgment that savings come from shedding protections.

The definition of 'covered laws' that follow the insurer's home state includes rating 'including medical underwriting,' so an insurer licensed in a state that allows health-based pricing could apply it to customers in states that forbid it, raising costs for people with health conditions.

The bill orders the Government Accountability Office to study, for five years, effects on the number of uninsured and underinsured, the availability and cost of coverage for people with preexisting conditions, the elimination or reduction of benefits, and fraud — a built-in admission that sponsors could not guarantee the outcome.

A secondary state's ability to challenge an insurer is narrowed: for most disputes, only the primary state can enforce the governing laws, and courts reviewing a secondary state's action must apply the primary state's laws.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but narrow: healthy people who rarely use care could buy cheaper, skinnier plans from a lightly regulated state. The costs fall broadly and unevenly: state-mandated benefits and rate protections disappear for anyone buying those plans, people with health conditions are left in shrinking, more expensive risk pools, and the state that knows the local market loses most of its power to act when something goes wrong. On balance, the bill was built around regulatory arbitrage for insurers more than around protection for people who buy insurance.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 2017, referred to the Senate health committee, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Dean Heller (R-NV) introduced the bill on June 29, 2017; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor — the cosponsor list stayed at zero.
The bill received no further action of any kind: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion action, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The bill would have amended the Public Health Service Act so the 'primary' state's laws govern an insurer's individual coverage sold in other states, exempting the insurer from the secondary state's laws that would regulate its operation, with the primary state holding sole enforcement jurisdiction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State insurance regulators kept full authority over the plans sold to their residents, and insurers gained no new ability to sell lightly regulated plans across state lines. Consumers were spared the risk-pool fragmentation and loss of state-mandated benefits the bill would have invited.

for.name: Sen. Dean Heller
for.role: U.S. Senator from Nevada; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on June 29, 2017.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (Chair Lamar Alexander)
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no recorded vote — the bill never generated enough support to move in the Republican-led Senate.

industries.note: The bill would have let insurers pick the state with the rules they like best — on required benefits, medical underwriting, and rate changes — and sell under those rules everywhere, exempting them from other states' oversight. The mechanism is regulatory arbitrage: the industry's gain comes from shedding state consumer protections, which is why the bill forces a warning label saying exactly that.

industries.industry: State insurance regulators and state governments
industries.note: States would have lost the power to apply their own coverage, benefit-mandate, and rating laws to policies sold to their residents, with enforcement shifted almost entirely to the insurer's chosen home state. States retained only narrow tools: taxation, financial examinations, insolvency funds, and fraud and claims-handling enforcement.
